name: King Cypress

location.address: World Cypress King Garden (世界柏树王园林), Bajie village (巴吉村), Bayi District, Nyingchi, Tibet Autonomous Region

access: Paid entry: a fenced, ticketed nature reserve/garden (¥15 entry per Baidu Baike) within the larger Bajie giant-cypress forest, reached by shared minibus, taxi or on foot from Bayi town (Nyingchi city). Best months April to October per the local source. Genuinely open to the public, a maintained tourist site rather than a wild grove.
transport: About 6-7 km southeast of Bayi town/Nyingchi city centre; shared minibuses run from town (~5 yuan) or taxi (~15 yuan one-way). No rail/air distances checked beyond that.
verify_notes: TWO INDEPENDENT SOURCES: English Wikipedia (King Cypress) and Baidu Baike (巨柏林), both describing the same individual, named, signature tree inside a small dedicated reserve near Bajie village, Nyingchi. They agree closely on coordinates (29.6229,94.4029 matches the lead exactly) and on height (~50m) and rough diameter (5.8m vs 'near 6m'). They DISAGREE on age: Wikipedia gives a calculated 2,600 years, Baidu gives 'over 3,200 years'; recorded both, not bridged into one figure. Girth recorded here (1820cm) is DERIVED from the stated diameter (5.8m x pi), not a directly measured circumference; note this for the writer rather than presenting it as a taped girth. Wikipedia/Baidu both describe it as the largest known specimen of Cupressus gigantea, the 'life tree' of Tönpa Shenrab Miwoche (founder of the Bön religion), locally called 'God of Tree'; pilgrims leave prayer flags and mani stones in the surrounding grove (0.1 km2 of ancient cypress averaging 44m tall). ALIVE/CURRENT: search results (not fetched as a source, so not cited above, only used as a lead) show Ctrip and other Chinese travel platforms currently listing '世界柏树王园林' (World Cypress King Garden) as an open, ticketed attraction in 2024-2025 travel guides and Linzhi peach-blossom-festival tour itineraries, consistent with a maintained, visited, living tree; a direct fetch of the Ctrip page 432'd twice and was abandoned per the two-attempts rule. NOT TO BE CONFUSED with a separate, newly surveyed 102.3m-tall Tibetan cypress found nearby in Bomi County's Tongmai town in 2023 (Peking University drone-lidar biodiversity survey, reported as 'Asia's tallest tree') - that is a different, unnamed specimen in a different township; no claim here that the King Cypress is that tree. DESTINATION TEST (this is an 'its own place' candidate, nearest published tree 1872km away): recommend SHIPPING as a standalone place. It carries real, longstanding tourist infrastructure (entrance fee, shuttle transport, marked reserve, tour-itinerary inclusion), a genuine religious/legendary pedigree tied to the founder of an entire religious tradition, and press coverage as the world's largest known specimen of its species and of a documented giant-tree region (Asia's-tallest-tree discovery nearby, same valley). This is comparable in kind to the Angel Oak or the Castagno dei Cento Cavalli: people build whole travel itineraries around this valley partly because of this tree. Not merely old or well-photographed, but a named pilgrimage/tourism destination in its own right.

name: Six-Dynasty Juniper

location.address: Northwest corner of the Sipailou campus, Southeast University, Xuanwu District, Nanjing, Jiangsu

access: Free; stands on the open campus of Southeast University, a public university whose historic Sipailou campus grounds visitors can walk. It is a well-known campus landmark and gathering spot for students, so treat access as free and open rather than restricted, though it sits on institutional grounds rather than a public park.
transport: Central Nanjing, Sipailou campus, Xuanwu District; walkable from central Nanjing metro stations (exact stop not independently confirmed this pass).
verify_notes: TWO INDEPENDENT SOURCES: English Wikipedia (Six-Dynasty Juniper) and Baidu Baike (六朝松), agreeing closely on coordinates (32.0589,118.7864, matching the lead), on the legend (said to have been planted personally by Emperor Wu of Liang, r.502-549, in the Liang imperial palace gardens; survived the Sui destruction of the city; the site later became the Ming Guozijian/Imperial Academy and then Southeast University), and on scale (12m tall, 6m crown). SPECIES: despite the common name meaning 'pine' in Chinese (song), Baidu Baike is explicit that this is actually Juniperus chinensis (a juniper/桧柏), a historical misnaming from when pine and cypress were not distinguished by name; recorded the correct species here rather than the lead's literal 'pine'. AGE: Wikipedia and Baidu both independently say 'over 1500 years' / 'approximately 1520 years'; recorded as a broad band (1450-1550) rather than a false-precision single number. GIRTH: Baidu gives trunk diameter as 99cm; girth_cm here (311) is DERIVED (99 x pi), not a taped circumference, flag this for the writer. CONDITION: Baidu Baike says the trunk interior is dead/hollow and the tree survives only through its outer bark, now supported by steel rods and concrete reinforcement; ALIVE evidence is current, per Baidu: 'following expert consultation and professional care, the ancient tree has sprouted new shoots and partially recovered its growth vigour.' A second attempt to fetch a 2022 Jiangsu English-language news piece on Nanjing's 'top 10 ancient trees' (which would likely have named this tree) failed on an expired TLS certificate; not pursued further per the two-attempts rule, but Chinese search results independently turned up multiple further press pieces referencing it as '金陵树王' ('Nanjing's tree king') and describing it as still lush as recently as 2017, consistent with (not itself cited as) the two sources above. DESTINATION TEST (this is an 'its own place' candidate, nearest published tree 823.8km away): recommend AGAINST shipping as a standalone place. This is a genuinely old, well-documented, alive and freely visitable campus tree with a real imperial legend, but it reads as a beloved local/campus curiosity rather than a reason to travel to Nanjing specifically; Nanjing itself is a major historic capital with its own strong draws (city wall, Ming tombs, Sun Yat-sen mausoleum) that would eclipse a single campus tree as 'the reason for the trip'. Better use: hold this as the seed tree for a future Nanjing city page (verified here, ready to use) rather than publish it alone; it does not need to carry a whole page by itself the way the King Cypress plausibly does.

name: Big Banyan Tree, Yangshuo

location.address: Big Banyan Tree Scenic Area (大榕树景区), on the Jinbao River, Gaotian Township, Yangshuo County, Guilin, Guangxi

access: Paid entry: a dedicated, ticketed scenic area (roughly 15-18 yuan solo, or a combo ticket with nearby Moon Hill), open 08:00-17:30 daily. Part of the well-trodden 'Ten Mile Gallery' cycling/tourist route south of Yangshuo town.
transport: About 7-7.5km south of Yangshuo County town, on the west/south bank of the Jinbao River near Moon Hill. Reachable by the Ten Mile Gallery sightseeing bus line from Yangshuo's Fengming Tourist Transport Center (~10 yuan), by bike along the Ten Mile Gallery road, or by bamboo raft on the Yulong River to Gongnong Bridge and a short walk.
verify_notes: TWO INDEPENDENT SOURCES (Baidu Baike and TravelChinaGuide) plus close corroboration from several other independent Chinese and English travel sources (CITS, TripAdvisor listing, Ctrip) all agreeing tightly: height 17m, girth ~7m (Baidu gives 7.05m precisely), age ~1400 years, planted in the Sui dynasty (581-618). Species given precisely by Baidu as Ficus concinna (Moraceae), not just 'banyan sp.' as the lead had it. ALIVE/CURRENT: this is an actively operating, ticketed tourist attraction with posted opening hours and a stated ~30-minute visit time, not a historical reference; strong current-alive evidence. HISTORY: this is the tree beneath which the 1960 film 'Liu Sanjie' (a landmark of Chinese cinema, the Zhuang folk-singer legend) staged its famous embroidered-ball love scene between Liu Sanjie and Aniu; a film-location marker stands under the tree today. Locally regarded as sacred by Zhuang residents, worshipped on new-moon and full-moon days. COLLECTIBLE POINT: passes easily, one specific, named, signposted tree with one obvious place to stand (and an old ferry crossing, 'Rongyin Gudu', at its foot). CONTAINER: neither Guilin nor Yangshuo is currently a published city in data/cities; this tree is well clear of the 30-minute day-trip boundary from Guilin city proper (Yangshuo town is roughly an hour from Guilin by road) so it would need Yangshuo as its own container rather than folding into a Guilin page, should Yangshuo ever be opened; not a placement decision made here, just flagged. This is a strong, low-risk verified delivery regardless of container: nothing here suggests holding it back.

name: Ginkgo of Shaolin Temple (Luohan Tree)

location.address: In front of the Hall of Heavenly Kings (Tianwang Dian), Shaolin Temple, Song Mountain, Dengfeng, Zhengzhou, Henan

access: Paid entry: Shaolin Temple is one of China's most visited religious/tourist sites, ticketed, open daily to the public.
transport: Within the Shaolin Temple complex on Song Mountain, near Dengfeng; the temple is a major tourist destination with regular bus and tour access from Dengfeng and Zhengzhou. No specific stop confirmed this pass.
verify_notes: ONE SOURCE DIRECTLY FETCHED AND CONFIRMED (m.sohu.com/a/203021767), describing a single, specific, named ginkgo standing in front of Tianwang Dian (the Hall of Heavenly Kings, one of the first halls on Shaolin's main axis): about 1,500 years old, 25m tall, 37m crown spread, described as 'the oldest existing tree in Dengfeng city', locally called the Luohan Tree (罗汉树) because it is a single male specimen (单体的雄树, per a second search-engine synthesis of the same claim, not independently fetched). A SECOND source could not be independently fetched this pass despite four attempts (hct.henan.gov.cn 403, zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/417233592 403, zh.wikipedia.org's Shaolin Temple article does not mention the tree at all, ichanfeng.com 404); search-engine summaries of those same pages (which are pointers, not sources per this project's rule, and not cited above) independently repeat the same age/location/dimensions/nickname, which is corroborating but not itself verification. FLAGGED for that reason: deliver on one directly-confirmed source rather than block. AMBIGUITY WORTH FLAGGING: a separate directly-fetched source (163.com, not used as a source for this entry since it does not corroborate this specific tree) describes a DIFFERENT 'King of Ginkgo Trees' designation applied to THREE ginkgos in the temple's pagoda courtyard (塔院), with the same finger-chan trunk-hole story attached. It is not established this pass whether the Tianwang Dian tree and the pagoda-courtyard trio are the same population described two ways or genuinely distinct groups; recommend a future pass resolve this with a direct Shaolin temple source (official site was unreachable, DNS failure) before writing the story, and lead with the Tianwang Dian tree since it is the one singled out by name and superlative ('oldest in Dengfeng'). COLLECTIBLE POINT: the Tianwang Dian tree passes as one specific, named, located tree, distinguished from Shaolin's many other old trees (200+ Song-dynasty cypresses elsewhere on the grounds, which do NOT qualify and are not part of this entry). HISTORY: trunk holes are locally attributed to monks practising 'one-finger Chan' and 'two-finger Chan' (yi zhi chan, er zhi chan) finger-strike training, a well-attested Shaolin legend (also reported, for the pagoda-courtyard trees, by the independently-fetched 163.com article) though not verified against a primary/scholarly source. PIN: location_precision is approximate because the lead's coordinate places the tree somewhere in the Shaolin Temple complex but was not independently checked against the Tianwang Dian's actual position; a future pass with satellite imagery or an OSM node for the hall itself could tighten this to confirmed. Girth not found anywhere, left empty.
